Solid and comprehensive axiomatic characterization that uniquely determines PASV through natural axioms (E+L+NP+M+MS+SCF+WP+EWU)
Principled theoretical framework showing correct reduction to PSV and WSV as special cases with clear explanation of why the |max⪯(Sₜ)| factor is necessary
Efficient and practical MCMC algorithm with local acceptance ratio evaluation (Lemma 4.1) enabling scalable computation on general DAGs
Novel and actionable diagnostic tool (priority sweeping) for practitioners to assess attribution sensitivity and identify unstable contributors
Comprehensive experiments on realistic data lineage scenarios (14-block DAG) and feature attribution with insightful analysis of non-monotone sweeping behavior (Table 3)
Interesting theoretical analysis of limiting regimes with appropriate caveats acknowledged via counterexample (Figure 3)
Clear and well-organized presentation with strong motivation (Figure 1) and accessible mathematical exposition overall
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is somewhat incremental—combines existing concepts (PSV + weighted sampling) in a principled but relatively natural way
Limited practical guidance for practitioners on specifying inputs: DAGs are constructed ad-hoc (LLM consultation in Appendix B.2.3) and λ weights chosen manually without principled methodology
Experimental validation shows flexibility but lacks evidence of practical superiority; no ground truth or expert validation that PASV produces better attributions than existing methods
Computational efficiency not quantified: no runtime comparisons, MCMC convergence analysis absent, and hyperparameter choices (B=100,000, τ=10,000) used empirically without justification
Limiting regime results (Propositions 3.13–3.14) have significant caveats; general DAGs don't guarantee translation to DAG edges (Figure 3 counterexample), limiting interpretability
Modest experimental scope with relatively small datasets (n=800 data points, n=12 features) and no evaluation of scalability to larger realistic ML applications
Sensitivity to DAG misspecification not explored; no guidance on validating or selecting between alternative DAG specifications empirically
Missing convergence analysis for MCMC algorithm (mixing times, effective sample size diagnostics) and no theoretical complexity guarantees provided

strengths: Well-motivated unification of hard precedence constraints and soft priority weights, addressing a genuine gap in combining PSV and WSV approaches
Clean reduction properties (Propositions 3.1-3.2) showing PASV recovers PSV and WSV as special cases, providing coherence to the generalization
Comprehensive axiomatic characterization via PROV and SCF framework with rigorous mathematical development
Practical priority sweeping diagnostic tool for sensitivity analysis that provides value to practitioners for identifying unstable attributions
Extensive experimental section with two diverse applications (data valuation, feature attribution) including detailed ablations and marginal contribution analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution (Equation 4) is the WSV formula extended to general DAGs via |max⪯(St)| normalization—a relatively straightforward incremental extension with limited conceptual insight

Axiomatization is circular in structure: axioms derive PROV, then SCF form is assumed (not derived), then additional axioms justify PASV. The SCF restriction lacks axiomatic justification, making this feel like post-hoc justification rather than derivation

Weak experimental validation lacking ground truth: experiments show PASV produces different allocations than PSV/WSV but don't validate these are actually correct or better. No comparison to recent related methods (Frye et al. 2020, Zheng et al. 2025)

Computational scalability claims unsupported: despite claiming 'scalable computation,' no mixing time analysis, convergence guarantees, or runtime comparisons provided. Large burn-in (B=100,000) and thinning (τ=10,000) suggest potential efficiency concerns

Critical unaddressed practical concern: DAG specification methodology is absent. Census Income DAG constructed via ChatGPT raises reproducibility issues. No principled approach for practitioners to construct valid DAGs

No guidance on weight parameter selection: soft priorities λ must be specified but the paper provides minimal guidance. Priority sweeping is a diagnostic tool but doesn't prescribe which weights to use

Non-monotone sensitivity responses unexpectedly appear in results (Figures 7, 12) contradicting intuition; post-hoc explanation in Appendix B.2.4 via 'amplifying/suppressing contexts' is ad-hoc rather than anticipated

Limiting regime analysis (Section 3.4) has important caveats: Propositions 3.13-3.14 only apply in specific cases; Figure 3 shows general case doesn't translate extreme weights to DAG edges, creating behavioral complexity

Synthetic experimental design: data lineage scenarios (MNIST/CIFAR10) are artificial without real-world validation. Simple utility functions (test accuracy); no sensitivity to parameter choices (k=20 for k-NN, b∈{2,8,32} appear arbitrary)
Disconnect between theory and practice: comprehensive axiomatization provides limited actionable insight for practitioners on when to use PASV versus alternatives

strengths: Unified theoretical framework elegantly combining hard precedence constraints and soft priority weights through a principled random-order value formulation, with rigorous axiomatic characterization (Theorem 3.12) that uniquely identifies PASV

Efficient MCMC-based computation via adjacent-swap Metropolis-Hastings (Algorithm 1) with local acceptance ratio evaluation (Lemma 4.1), enabling scalable handling of general DAGs that prior methods (e.g., WSV) could not accommodate

Novel and practically useful priority sweeping diagnostic tool that enables sensitivity analysis by varying individual weights while preserving DAG structure, providing actionable robustness insights unavailable from single-point estimates

Insightful analysis of limiting regimes (Propositions 3.13-3.14) clarifying when extreme priority weights translate to new DAG edges, supported by instructive counterexamples and empirical validation against theoretical predictions

Thoughtfully designed experiments with realistic data lineage structures; marginal contribution analysis (Figure 5, middle) provides interpretable explanations for PASV vs. PSV differences through position-dependent effects

Clear presentation with strong visual aids, comprehensive implementation details, and honest treatment of limitations (counterexamples, non-monotone responses); full LLM transcript enables reproducibility and transparency
Correct recovery of PSV and WSV as special cases (Propositions 3.1-3.2), demonstrating that the unification genuinely generalizes prior work without losing important special structure
weaknesses: Experimental scale is modest (data valuation: n=800; feature attribution: n=12) with no large-scale validation; scalability claims lack empirical support (no wall-clock timing comparisons or convergence analysis as function of n or DAG complexity)

Computational aspects underexplored: burn-in and thinning hyperparameters stated but not justified; no convergence diagnostics (effective sample size, autocorrelation, R-hat) or analysis of MCMC mixing time as function of |Π_⪯|; missing complexity bounds for convergence rate

DAG specification subjectivity: Census Income DAG constructed via LLM consultation (Appendix B.2.3) with acknowledged non-causal interpretation; no robustness analysis of sensitivity to DAG misspecification; MNIST/CIFAR10 data lineage is synthetic and artificial

Limited practical guidance on weight selection: paper motivates λ (trust, cost, risk) but provides minimal concrete advice for practitioners; no demonstration of real-world adoption or that practitioners actually need this combination of features

Incomplete experimental validation: no statistical significance tests between methods; missing ablations on convergence criteria, utility function choices, and impact of weight specifications; no comparison with other precedence-respecting methods or with performance when ignoring precedence

Technical presentation gaps: restriction to SCF form (Eq. 6) lacks formal justification for why only these distributions should be considered; Axiom MS (Maximal Support) is novel relative to classical Shapley axioms but implications deserve deeper discussion; Lemma 4.1's claim of 'local' information is slightly misleading

Scope limitations: the combination of general precedence constraints with per-player soft weights is somewhat specialized; unclear how many practitioners need both features simultaneously; generality may reduce practical impact compared to addressing one aspect thoroughly

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of standard Shapley values in settings with precedence constraints and priority considerations
Rigorous theoretical framework with principled axiomatization showing PASV is uniquely characterized by natural axioms
Elegant theoretical contributions including PROV/SCF framework and limiting case analysis
Solid algorithmic development with efficient MCMC sampler achieving O(n²) mixing time and local acceptance ratio optimization
Comprehensive experimental validation across data valuation and feature attribution tasks with priority sweeping diagnostic
Thorough reproducibility support with detailed implementations, algorithms, and extensive appendices with proofs and additional experiments
Good presentation of technical content overall with clear motivation and well-structured development
weaknesses: Limited practical validation—experiments primarily show PASV *can* differentiate based on weights, not that resulting valuations are superior; no compelling cases where ignoring precedence yields demonstrably wrong results
Incremental technical contributions that combine existing ideas (precedence Shapley, weighted Shapley, MCMC sampling) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Critical practical guidance is missing: no principled methodology for DAG construction (Census Income DAG via ChatGPT raises concerns), no guidance for weight specification (λ = b^c appears arbitrary), no sensitivity analysis to weight misspecification

Scalability concerns for realistic applications—experiments use closed-form utilities or small datasets; proxy-based estimator requires O(n²) memory (tens of GB for n=2048); no experiments with expensive utilities (e.g., deep learning)

Theoretical gaps including lack of intuition for why this hard/soft priority combination is optimal, no sample complexity or convergence rate analysis, and Propositions 3.13-3.14 conditions are quite specific
Limited experimental scope: data valuation only on MNIST/CIFAR10 with k-NN, feature attribution only on Census Income with single architecture, no comparison with other recent data valuation methods

Presentation could be more accessible—dense technical content, axiomatization presented as outline before details, SCF framework notation-heavy without sufficient intuition, figures 5 and 19 difficult to parse

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies real limitations of standard Shapley values when contributors are dependent or should be weighted by trust/risk factors. Motivation for unifying precedence constraints and soft priorities is compelling.

Elegant theoretical unification: PASV framework successfully unifies PSV (precedence-only) and WSV (weight-only for ordered partitions) as special cases within a single coherent random-order value framework.
Solid axiomatization: Progression from base axioms through PROV, SCF factorization, and boundary case axioms to characterize PASV is technically rigorous with properly proven theorems (3.8, 3.12).

Insightful limiting regime analysis: Section 3.4 provides valuable intuition about how extreme priority weights interact with hard precedence constraints, with formal results (Propositions 3.13-3.14).

Efficient and well-analyzed computation: Adjacent-swap MH sampler is properly designed; empirical analysis showing O(n²) mixing in practice (rather than worst-case O(n³ log n)) is valuable. Comprehensive comparison of direct MC vs. proxy estimators.
Practical diagnostic tool: Priority sweeping provides an intuitive sensitivity analysis mechanism for practitioners to assess robustness to weight specification.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The formula p^(⪯,λ)(π) ∝ ∏ λ_{πₜ}|max⪯(Sₜ)| / Σ λₖ is relatively straightforward once the problem is formulated. Core contribution is problem formulation rather than fundamentally new techniques; mainly adapts existing ideas (random order values, MCMC, axiomatization style).

Unconvincing experimental validation: Data valuation experiments mainly show PASV interpolates between uniform Shapley and PSV as parameter b varies—unsurprising and not demonstrating clear superiority. Claim of 'structure-faithful allocations' lacks quantitative validation. Feature attribution tested on only one dataset (Census Income) with DAG constructed via ChatGPT (somewhat arbitrary).

Insufficient practical guidance: No principled method for choosing λ values in practice—they appear ad-hoc in experiments (λ = b^c with arbitrary exponents). DAG specification is acknowledged as difficult but inadequately addressed; sensitivity analysis (Figure 19) shows method can be sensitive to DAG changes.

Non-monotone behavior under priority changes: Priority sweeps show counterintuitive non-monotone responses (e.g., U-shaped capital-gain value in Figure 17). While explained via feature interactions, this raises interpretability concerns and may trouble practitioners. No discussion of whether this is feature or limitation.

Significant theoretical gaps: No convergence rate analysis beyond empirical mixing time; no sample complexity bounds or error analysis for Monte Carlo estimation; no formal guidance on number of samples needed for reliable estimates. Axiomatization feels post-hoc (designed to pick PASV from family) rather than deriving from first principles.

Weak experimental comparisons: No direct comparison to Asymmetric Shapley (Frye et al. 2020) beyond ordered partition reduction. Missing comparisons to Group Shapley (Lee et al. 2025) and replication-robust methods (Han et al. 2022) mentioned in introduction.

Unclear computational scalability: Figure 9 shows ~10k unique utility evaluations for n=512 with synthetic utilities. Real-world scalability unclear for expensive utilities (e.g., model retraining). Computational cost relative to benefit not convincingly established.

Unclear practical motivation: Paper does not articulate clear scenarios where PASV's added complexity (specifying both precise DAG and λ values) is justified over simpler alternatives. When should practitioners actually use PASV?

strengths: Well-motivated unification of hard precedence constraints and soft individual weights, addressing real practical needs in data valuation and feature attribution
Rigorous axiomatic characterization with novel State-Choice Factorization concept that elegantly separates global structure effects from individual weighting
Practical contribution of 'priority sweeping' sensitivity diagnostic providing actionable robustness analysis for practitioners
Theoretically sound: clean reduction results showing PSV and WSV as special cases; insightful limiting case analysis (Propositions 3.13-3.14) on extreme weights
Computationally competent: well-designed MCMC Algorithm 1 with efficient local acceptance ratio computation; empirical mixing time O(n²) with limited weight effect
Handles general DAGs (meaningful generalization over WSV's ordered partitions); comprehensive experimental validation with data valuation and feature attribution applications
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: core formula (Eq. 4) is straightforward generalization of weighted Shapley to general DAGs; combines existing technical machinery (posets, weighted Shapley, MCMC) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas

Insufficient baseline comparisons: missing empirical comparison with recent data valuation methods (Beta Shapley, Data Banzhaf, replication-robust variants) cited in paper; only compares against foundational SV/PSV/WSV

Critical practical issues unresolved: DAG construction relies on ChatGPT (Section F.3); no principled procedure for weight λ selection, leaving practitioners with ad-hoc guidance; these gaps limit real-world deployment despite theoretical soundness

Computational complexity analysis incomplete: mixing time analysis primarily empirical without formal guarantees under weighted setting; scalability modest (n≤2048 for proxy method); proxy-based variant requires tens of GB peak memory, raising practical concerns
Experimental scale and scope limited: data valuation uses n=800 points, feature attribution n=12 features; more ambitious experiments needed; limited ablation studies on method sensitivity

Axiomatization section (3.3) is mathematically dense and lacks intuitive explanation; missing worked toy example; U-shaped priority sweep patterns (Section F.4.1) explained post-hoc rather than predicted
